paras: The attack on Peter Stark by militiamen at Griffin, Georgia, took place on the afternoon of June 29, 1903, when soldiers of the Second Regiment, encamped in the town, rushed Stark, a Black man, on Hill street after a dispute with one of their sergeants. Citizens and police rescued him, and the mayor dismissed the cases against all parties. The Savannah Morning News reported that a clash between soldiers and townspeople had been narrowly averted.
The incident occurred on the closing day of a militia encampment at Griffin, whose companies included the Columbus Light Guards.

According to a Griffin dispatch, Stark, "it is claimed," insulted a sergeant of the Second Regiment and was "promptly struck over the head." Stark then drew a long knife but, instead of attacking the sergeant, backed out of the crowd. Seeing the knife, "a large number of soldiers" ran to their comrade's aid and were "about to do serious personal violence" to Stark when a few citizens arrived and, with the police, rescued him from the "infuriated soldiers." The correspondent added that Stark would certainly have been killed had he cut the sergeant.

All parties were arrested and tried before Mayor Bailey, who dismissed the cases, and police escorted Stark to a place of safety. That night no passes were issued and no one was allowed to leave camp after 7 o'clock, and the camp was to break up at noon the next day.

The only account found ran in the Savannah Morning News on June 30 under the headlines "NEGRO DREW KNIFE" and "SOLDIERS AT GRIFFIN PROMPTLY ASSAILED HIM," followed by "THE MAN WAS RESCUED FROM THE INFURIATED SOLDIERS." The story led with Stark's knife, qualified the insult as only "claimed," and credited "a few cool heads" with preventing serious trouble. It appeared as part of the paper's encampment news, alongside a society drill and the closing dress parade. No Black-press coverage of the incident was found.
The dispatch describes the knife two ways, saying first that Stark backed away without attacking and later that he "attempted to use the knife" but did not.

reader.title: Attack on Peter Stark by militiamen at Griffin, Georgia
bases: A sergeant struck Stark and a large number of soldiers rushed him intending 'serious personal violence' before citizens and police intervened (A1); no wider threat or campaign is described.
Only one report, a Griffin dispatch in the Savannah Morning News, was found (A1); searches of both presses found no other account.

accounts.label: Griffin correspondent
accounts.gist: Stark, it was claimed, insulted a sergeant and was struck; he drew a knife but backed out of the crowd, and soldiers rushing him were stopped by citizens and police. The paper added that he would have been killed had he cut the sergeant.

framing.detail: Headlines 'NEGRO DREW KNIFE' and 'SOLDIERS AT GRIFFIN PROMPTLY ASSAILED HIM' put Stark's knife first, while the text called the soldiers 'infuriated', praised the rescuers' 'cool heads', and qualified the insult as 'claimed'.

versions.value: Stark drew the knife but 'instead of attacking the sergeant, backed out of the crowd'
Stark 'attempted to use the knife, but, fortunately, did not do so'

conflicts.note: The same dispatch describes Stark's handling of the knife two ways; both agree he did not cut anyone.
